questions.q: Why does Chapter 7 check whether the discrepancy also appears at a different quarter boundary, not just Q3's?
options: To make the investigation take longer
If the gap reappears at a different quarter, it rules out a one-time data entry mistake and points at the formula's logic itself, not any particular quarter's data
Because Power BI only stores one quarter of data at a time
Because Tableau requires checking multiple quarters before publishing
questions.explain: A gap that recurs at a different boundary is strong evidence the problem is structural — in how the formula is written — not a one-off data issue.

questions.q: What does the isolation formula =SUMIFS(Data[LineTotal], Data[OrderDate], DATE(2013,10,1)) actually test for?
options: The total for the entire month of October
Every line where OrderDate is exactly October 1st, 2013 — the exact boundary day in question
The total for all of Q4 2013
Every line with a blank OrderDate value
questions.explain: Isolating exactly the boundary date lets you confirm whether orders on that single day are being included where they shouldn't be, and whether that amount matches the discrepancy.

questions.q: What is the real bug in the original SUMIFS formula from Lesson 21?
options: It sums the wrong column entirely
Its upper bound uses <= DATE(2013,10,1), an inclusive boundary that includes October 1st — the first day of Q4 — in a formula meant to total only Q3
It is missing a lower bound entirely
DATE(2013,10,1) refers to the wrong year
questions.explain: Using <= on the upper bound includes the boundary date itself, which belongs to the next quarter, not the one being totaled.

questions.q: Why were Power BI's and Tableau's totals never vulnerable to this specific mistake?
options: They don't use dates in their calculations at all

Both ultimately filter through dw.DimDate's discrete calendar rows — one row per real day, each belonging to exactly one quarter — which has no boundary-inclusion ambiguity for a human to get wrong the way a SUMIFS date comparison does
They use a completely different fact table than Excel
They were manually checked by a human before publishing, unlike Excel
questions.explain: A discrete calendar dimension table assigns each day to exactly one quarter with no ambiguity, unlike a continuous date-range comparison in a spreadsheet formula.

questions.q: What is the exact fix for the original buggy formula?
options: Change the sum range from Data[LineTotal] to Data[OrderQty]
Change the upper bound's comparison from <= to <, making the range half-open instead of inclusive on both ends
Remove the upper bound criterion entirely
Change DATE(2013,10,1) to DATE(2013,9,30)
questions.explain: Changing <= to < makes the range half-open — inclusive of the start, exclusive of the end — which correctly excludes October 1st from the Q3 total.
